story: USGS puts undiscovered North Slope gas at 96 trillion cubic feet, and the AI data center plans that would burn it on the Slope while Alaska LNG still lacks a final investment decision

claims.claim: The USGS estimates a mean of 96 trillion cubic feet of undiscovered, technically recoverable conventional gas in the Northern Alaska Province, 96,094 billion cubic feet in its table, about 96.1 trillion.
claims.verbatim: estimated undiscovered, technically recoverable mean conventional resources of 96 trillion cubic feet of gas in the Northern Alaska Province.
claims.notes: Abstract on the pubs.usgs.gov landing page and the PDF https://pubs.usgs.gov/fs/2026/3031/fs20263031.pdf (page 1). Table 1 total is 96,094 BCFG. Corroborated by Interior's release, Alaska Public Media (KNBA) and the Alaska Beacon via ADN. Title is 'Assessment of Undiscovered Conventional Gas Resources in the Northern Alaska Province, 2026', lead author William H. Craddock.

claims.claim: The USGS range for undiscovered North Slope gas runs from 17,326 billion cubic feet at the F95 level to 276,681 billion cubic feet at the F5 level.
claims.verbatim: range from 17,326 to 276,681 BCFG
claims.notes: PDF page 4, Undiscovered Resources Summary, and the Table 1 totals row (17,326 / 66,357 / 276,681 / 96,094 BCFG for F95 / F50 / F5 / mean). NUMBER CORRECTION: 276,681 BCFG rounds to 276.7 tcf. The Alaska Beacon/ADN wrote '276.6 trillion' (truncated) and the scout attributed the range to Alaska Public, which does not print it. Deck should write 17.3 to 276.7 trillion cubic feet, or 'about 17 to 277 trillion'. The full sentence also contains an en dash in 'F95-F5', so the verbatim is the dash-free substring.

claims.claim: In the USGS tables, F95 means a 95 percent chance of at least the amount shown.
claims.verbatim: F95 represents a 95-percent chance of at least the amount tabulated; other fractiles are defined similarly.
claims.notes: Table 1 header note, PDF pages 4 and 5. Use it to explain the range in plain words. F5 is therefore a 5 percent chance of at least 276,681 BCFG. Results are 'fully risked estimates'.

claims.claim: The USGS estimates a mean of 549 million barrels of undiscovered natural gas liquids in the Northern Alaska Province.
claims.verbatim: The mean undiscovered natural gas liquids resource is 549 million barrels of natural gas liquids (MMBNGL), with an F95
claims.notes: PDF page 4. The NGL range is 101 to 1,552 MMBNGL (Table 1 totals). Neither Interior's release, Alaska Public nor ADN mentions NGLs.

claims.claim: The same USGS assessment puts the mean undiscovered oil resource of the province at about 17 billion barrels.
claims.verbatim: The mean undiscovered oil resource is 17,099 million barrels of oil (MMBO), or 17 billion barrels of oil
claims.notes: PDF page 4. The USGS says this oil figure 'reaffirms recent oil-focused appraisals' (2017 and 2020). It came from applying earlier petroleum system framework models, so it is a by-product of the gas assessment and not a new oil assessment. Range is 3,044 to 46,617 MMBO.

claims.claim: The USGS divided the province into 21 assessment units in three sets, one for each stratigraphic sequence.
claims.verbatim: The USGS defined 21 assessment units (AUs) in three sets
claims.notes: PDF page 2. 8 Ellesmerian, 7 Beaufortian and 6 Brookian AUs (Figures 1, 3, 4). Table 1 title reads 'Results for 21 conventional assessment units in the Northern Alaska Province.' The largest single mean is the Beaufortian Deformed Central AU, 12,921 BCFG of nonassociated gas.

claims.claim: The assessment covers the whole province from the Brooks Range front north to the federal waters boundary about 3 miles off the Arctic coast, so it includes onshore land and state waters.
claims.verbatim: boundary with Federal waters offshore of the arctic coast (generally about 3 miles [5 kilometers] from the shoreline), and the international border between the United States and Canada in northern Alaska.
claims.notes: PDF page 1. Preceding words: 'The spatial scope is provincewide, covering the entire area between the Brooks Range front, the Submerged Lands Act' boundary. The maps also include NPR-A and the ANWR 1002 area. 'Onshore and state waters' is the plain-language reading of the Submerged Lands Act boundary. The fact sheet doesn't use the words 'state waters', so prose should say 'out to about 3 miles offshore'. Federal offshore waters are excluded. The Beacon/ADN piece says it covers 'the entire North Slope, including the 23 million-acre petroleum reserve'.

claims.claim: The estimate counts gas found with oil as well as gas found without oil, and covers conventional resources only.
claims.verbatim: This estimate includes gas that is associated with oil accumulations (associated gas) as well as gas that is not associated with any large accumulation of oil (nonassociated gas).
claims.notes: PDF page 1. 'Conventional' is in the title. The Beacon/ADN piece confirms the report 'considers only conventional oil and gas' and leaves out unconventional resources.

claims.claim: The USGS says that as of 2026 there is no way to bring North Slope gas to market at large commercial scale.
claims.verbatim: However, as of 2026, there is no method for bringing natural gas to markets at large commercial scales, although considerable known accumulations of gas resources exist in the province
claims.notes: PDF page 1, Introduction. Corroborated by the Alaska Beacon via ADN (October 23rd): the gas '...remains stranded on the North Slope, hundreds of miles from any market.' The USGS adds that 'several mechanisms for bringing the gas to markets have been proposed' and cites 8 Star Alaska (Alaska LNG). Data centers aren't mentioned in the fact sheet, Interior's release, Alaska Public or ADN. The deck should present the data center link as its own framing and not as something the agency said.

claims.claim: Most gas produced alongside North Slope oil is pumped back underground to keep reservoir pressure up.
claims.verbatim: Most gas that is coproduced with oil from the Northern Alaska Province is reinjected into reservoirs for pressure management
claims.notes: PDF page 1. USGS cites the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission (2026).

claims.claim: The USGS puts the estimated ultimate recovery of the Prudhoe Bay gas cap at about 25 trillion cubic feet.
claims.verbatim: the gas cap in the Prudhoe Bay field, which has an estimated ultimate recovery (EUR) value of about 25 trillion cubic feet of gas (TCFG)
claims.notes: PDF page 1. Next item: 'Point Thomson field, which has an estimated EUR value of 8 TCFG'. These are known accumulations and not part of the 96 tcf undiscovered figure.

claims.claim: Interior says the 96 trillion cubic feet estimate is nearly three times the roughly 35 trillion cubic feet of proven North Slope gas reserves.
claims.verbatim: This is nearly three times the roughly 35 trillion cubic feet (TCFG) of proven gas reserves on the North Slope.
claims.notes: Same release as https://www.doi.gov/node/68126 (both fetched). The 35 tcf figure is in Interior's release and not in the USGS fact sheet. Corroborated by Alaska Public ('roughly 35 trillion cubic feet of proven gas reserves') and the Beacon/ADN ('35 trillion cubic feet of known reserves, most of which lie within the Greater Prudhoe Bay Unit'). Sanity check: 96/35 = 2.7, so 'nearly three times' holds. Conflict: the Alaska Current (October 3rd) writes 'nearly 30 trillion cubic feet of proven natural gas reserves in Prudhoe Bay'. Use 35 tcf from Interior, and call it 'proven' or 'known' rather than 'discovered'.

claims.claim: The Interior Department announced the USGS North Slope gas assessment on October 21st.
claims.verbatim: USGS Releases Assessment of Undiscovered Natural Gas Resources in Alaska's North Slope
claims.notes: Release is datelined Reston, Va., 10/21/2026. The USGS publication date is also October 21st (pubs.usgs.gov). Inside the window. The release ties the assessment to Executive Order 14153 and Secretary's Order 3422.

claims.claim: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said Alaska's natural gas reserves can supply affordable, reliable, secure energy to Americans and U.S. allies.
claims.verbatim: Alaska's natural gas reserves can supply affordable, reliable, secure energy to Americans and our South Pacific allies
claims.suggested_phrasing: Burgum said in Interior's release that Alaska's gas 'can supply affordable, reliable, secure energy to Americans and our South Pacific allies'.
claims.notes: This is a fragment of a longer quote of about 85 words. The apostrophe is curly on the page and straightened here. It's advocacy, so attribute it and don't use it as fact. Quote only this exact fragment.

claims.claim: USGS Director Ned Mamula said the agency's gas assessments point to resources industry hasn't discovered yet.
claims.verbatim: USGS natural gas assessments point to resources that industry hasn't discovered yet.
claims.notes: Fragment of a quote of about 50 words. Apostrophe straightened. Another verified fragment from the same quote: 'we estimate there are significant undiscovered gas resources in the North Slope of Alaska'.

claims.claim: USGS energy resources program coordinator Alicia Lindauer said the estimate is almost as much gas as the United States consumes in three years.
claims.verbatim: Lindauer said that's almost as much gas as the nation consumes over three years.
claims.suggested_phrasing: A USGS official told reporters that's nearly three years of U.S. gas use.
claims.notes: The comparison doesn't appear in the USGS fact sheet or Interior's release. It comes from a news briefing as reported by two independent outlets. Corroborated by the Alaska Beacon via ADN (October 23rd): '...just under three years' worth of U.S. natural gas consumption.' Attribute it to the USGS official, not to the assessment. Sanity check: U.S. use is roughly 32 to 33 tcf a year, so 96 tcf is about 2.9 years, which is consistent. Alaska Public also notes that USGS assessments 'do not estimate whether resources can be extracted profitably.'

claims.claim: The Alaska Beacon reports that this is the first resource assessment for natural gas covering the whole North Slope.
claims.verbatim: It is the first North Slope-wide resource assessment for natural gas.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (Yereth Rosen), published by Anchorage Daily News
claims.suggested_phrasing: the first gas assessment to cover the whole North Slope, according to the Alaska Beacon
claims.notes: Neither the USGS fact sheet nor Interior's release says 'first'. The fact sheet does say its scope is 'provincewide', and earlier USGS gas work covered parts of the Slope (western North Slope 2021, central 2020, NPR-A 2017). That supports the reading, but it's the outlet's characterization. Attribute it, or say 'province-wide' (which is verifiable on the fact sheet) instead of 'first'.

claims.claim: Alaska DNR's Division of Oil and Gas made a preliminary decision to offer STAK Energy Corporation a 50-year lease of state land under ADL 422741.
claims.verbatim: has made a Preliminary Decision to offer a 50-year lease
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas (Online Public Notice)
claims.notes: BACKGROUND, outside the window. Notice title is 'Public Notice of Preliminary Decision: ADL 422741, Land Lease Application, STAK Energy Corporation'. It was reissued on June 17th as notice 224224 with an extended deadline. No final decision was found. Anchorage Press (July 3rd) says DNR will assess comments before a final decision.

claims.claim: The proposed STAK Energy lease covers a 715.4-acre parcel.
claims.verbatim: 715.4-acre parcel
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas (Online Public Notice)
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. Notice 224224 (June 17th) also reads '715.4 acre parcel'. Anchorage Press describes it as 'roughly one square mile' (715 acres is about 1.1 square miles, so that's consistent).

claims.claim: The STAK Energy lease site sits beside the Dalton Highway about 26 miles south of Deadhorse.
claims.verbatim: The proposed lease site is located adjacent to the Dalton Highway approximately 26 miles south of Deadhorse.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas (Online Public Notice)
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. Anchorage Press says 'some 25 miles'. Use DNR's 26.

claims.claim: DNR describes the STAK Energy project as a commercial natural gas-powered energy facility that includes modular high-performance computing units.
claims.verbatim: a commercial natural gas-powered energy facility, including modular high-performance computing units
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas (Online Public Notice)
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. The notice also says 'on-site natural gas power generation infrastructure'. It doesn't use the words 'data center', 'AI' or 'cloud', and it states no GW figure or investment figure. Attachments (preliminary decision PDF, development plan) returned HTTP 503 and couldn't be read.

claims.claim: DNR extended the comment deadline on the STAK Energy lease to July 17th.
claims.verbatim: no later than 4:30 PM Alaska Daylight Time on July 17, 2026
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas (Online Public Notice)
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. The original deadline in notice 223817 was June 15th. Anchorage Press confirms DNR 'has since extended the deadline an extra month, to July 17.'

claims.claim: State officials received more than 500 public comments on the proposed North Slope data center and power plant.
claims.verbatim: In July, state officials received more than 500 public comments on a proposed North Slope data center and power plant.
claims.notes: Independently corroborated by Anchorage Press, Nathaniel Herz, July 3rd (https://www.anchoragepress.com/data-center-critics-flood-alaska-land-managers-with-opposition-to-north-slope-project/): 'More than 500 public comments were received before a preliminary deadline set by the Alaska Department of Natural Resources'. The scout's northernjournal.com URL now redirects to anchoragepress.com. No primary comment count was reachable.

claims.claim: STAK Energy's generators could produce a gigawatt or more of power, according to the Anchorage Press.
claims.verbatim: Its generators could produce a gigawatt or more of power
claims.suggested_phrasing: could generate a gigawatt or more, according to the Anchorage Press
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. Single secondary source, and the DNR notice states no capacity. The article says this is about 30 percent more than urban Alaska's peak grid demand. The scout's '1 to 3 GW' isn't supported anywhere fetched, so it's KILLED.

claims.claim: STAK Energy chief strategy officer John Boyle said the project would cost more than $10 billion.
claims.verbatim: which Boyle said would cost more than $10 billion
claims.suggested_phrasing: a project the developer says would cost more than $10 billion
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. This is the developer's own figure, so present it as the developer's claim. Boyle was Alaska DNR commissioner from 2023 to 2025 (same article), which is worth noting because DNR is the agency deciding the lease. The DNR notice gives no dollar figure. Burgum's 'want to drop 10 billion' (KUAC, October 15th) wasn't verified here.

claims.claim: The Anchorage Press reports the STAK Energy power would serve artificial intelligence and cloud computing customers.
claims.verbatim: power plants that could support artificial intelligence and cloud computing
claims.suggested_phrasing: pitched to AI and cloud customers
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. The article also says the company would sell power to 'hyperscalers' and would use 'abundant natural gas from nearby North Slope oil fields'. DNR's own wording is 'modular high-performance computing units' (C21). KUAC calls it 'a proposed North Slope data center and power plant' (C23).

claims.claim: The North Slope Borough and Twenty First Century Utilities partnered to create North Slope Power.
claims.verbatim: The North Slope Borough and Twenty First Century Utilities have partnered to create North Slope Power
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. Corroborated by the Alaska Current (Lauren Windsor, October 3rd), which describes a borough resolution under which 'the Borough would initially maintain a majority ownership interest' and says the borough 'committed another $5 million in public funds' in March. No primary borough document was fetched.

claims.claim: North Slope Power proponents describe a 3 gigawatt first phase that could expand to 10 gigawatts.
claims.verbatim: The proponents said it would be a 3 gigawatt first phase that could be expanded to 10 gigawatts.
claims.suggested_phrasing: proponents say 3 gigawatts at first, and up to 10 gigawatts eventually
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. These are the proponents' plans, not built capacity. Corroborated by the Alaska Current (October 3rd): 'a 3 gigawatt natural gas plant with plans to scale to a world record-breaking 10 gigawatts'. 3 GW is 3,000 MW and 10 GW is 10,000 MW. Neither source gives a cost or an annual gas burn.

claims.claim: North Slope Power is designed to supply colocated AI data centers and industrial load.
claims.verbatim: Designed to power colocated AI data centers and industrial load
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. Corroborated by the Alaska Current (October 3rd): 'to deliver electricity to colocated AI data centers'.

claims.claim: Proponents say North Slope Power would be the world's largest natural gas power plant, sited near Prudhoe Bay.
claims.verbatim: create the world's largest natural gas power plant near Prudhoe Bay
claims.suggested_phrasing: pitched as the largest gas power plant in the world, near Prudhoe Bay
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. Size claim is corroborated by the Alaska Current: 'larger than any natural gas plant currently operating in the world'. The Prudhoe Bay location is single-sourced (Cole). The Current only says it would tap Prudhoe Bay reserves. Cole gives the reserves as 'more than 35 trillion cubic feet' and the Current as 'nearly 30', so don't use either figure.

claims.claim: President Trump called Alaska LNG a U.S. federal government project in a social media post.
claims.verbatim: the Alaska LNG megaproject is now "a U.S. Federal Government Project."
claims.notes: Page shows 'Published: October 20, 2026', although the URL path says 10/19. ADN says Trump posted 'last week' on Truth Social, which puts the post before October 19th. The scout's 'October 19th' date is NOT verified, so don't date the post. Curly quotes straightened. Truth Social primary not fetched. ADN says federal ownership is possible but what the designation means is unsettled.

claims.claim: The Alaska LNG plan calls for an 800-mile pipeline carrying 20 million metric tons of gas a year from the North Slope to an export terminal on Cook Inlet.
claims.verbatim: The Alaska LNG project envisions an 800-mile pipeline carrying 20 million metric tons of natural gas per year from the North Slope to an export terminal on Cook Inlet.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), published by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: 800 miles is corroborated by ADN October 20th ('an 800-mile gas pipeline', phase one serving Alaskans) and by the Beacon/ADN October 23rd. The 20 million tonnes figure appears only in this article among the pages fetched. It's the long-standing design figure, but it's single-sourced here, so confidence is lower if the deck uses it.

claims.claim: Official estimates put the Alaska LNG project's cost between $44.5 billion and $54.5 billion.
claims.verbatim: Official estimates state that the project will cost between $44.5 billion to $54.5 billion.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), published by Alaska Public Media
claims.suggested_phrasing: officially estimated at $44.5 billion to $54.5 billion, with unofficial estimates above $65 billion
claims.notes: This is a projection. The same article says unofficial estimates have exceeded $65 billion. ADN October 20th: 'Glenfarne says Alaska LNG could cost up to $55 billion.' That's consistent at the top end. ADN does not print the $44.5B figure, contrary to the scout merge.

claims.claim: Private developer Glenfarne owns 75 percent of Alaska LNG and the state-controlled Alaska Gasline Development Corp. owns the rest.
claims.verbatim: Seventy-five percent of the pipeline project is currently owned by the private developer Glenfarne, and the remainder is owned by the state-controlled Alaska Gasline Development Corp.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), published by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: Corroborated by ADN October 20th: 'the state's Alaska Gasline Development Corp. will retain its 25% stake in the project', and Glenfarne's 75 percent could be reduced or eliminated under federal involvement while Glenfarne remains developer.

claims.claim: Alaska LNG's final investment decision, first proposed for last year, still hasn't been made.
claims.verbatim: That decision, originally proposed for last year, has still not been made.
claims.notes: In context 'that decision' is the final investment decision. Consistent with the USGS statement that there is no large-scale method to market (C09) and with the Beacon's 'remains stranded' (October 23rd).

claims.claim: Taiwan's economic affairs ministry said state-owned CPC will invest up to $4.4 billion in the Alaska LNG pipeline project.
claims.verbatim: will invest up to $4.4 billion in the pipeline project
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), published by Alaska Public Media
claims.suggested_phrasing: Taiwan says it will invest up to $4.4 billion, with terms still to be set
claims.notes: Not final. The article says 'Specific investment arrangements, equity stakes and related terms will be' settled later, and that a preliminary heads of agreement could follow. ADN October 20th reports Trump claimed $4.5 billion and Taiwan says no investment is finalized. Use the ministry's $4.4 billion. Taiwan ministry primary not fetched.

claims.claim: AGDC president Frank Richards said negotiations were nearing conclusion on price and term for 6 million metric tons of gas a year for Taiwan.
claims.verbatim: negotiations have continued and are nearing conclusion on price and term" "for the 6 million metric tons of gas per year that
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), published by Alaska Public Media
claims.suggested_phrasing: about 6 million tonnes a year, still under negotiation
claims.notes: Richards made the remark to ADN and the Beacon relayed it. The verbatim was returned as joined fragments; the safe exact substring is 'for the 6 million metric tons of gas per year'. The ministry put Taiwan's purchase at up to 30% of production. Sanity check: 6 of 20 Mtpa is 30 percent, which is consistent.

claims.claim: Korean officials said the Alaska pipeline isn't yet confirmed as part of South Korea's U.S. investment deal.
claims.verbatim: Korean officials said after the Trump administration announcement that the Alaska pipeline is not yet confirmed to be part of the
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), published by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: Corroborated by ADN October 20th (South Korean leaders are reviewing the project and no plan is finalized, against Trump's claim of about $50 billion) and by the Beacon/ADN October 23rd (Korea 'evaluating possible participation in the Alaska LNG project').

claims.claim: DNR issued a preliminary decision proposing to convey about 19,950 acres of state land near Houston to AIDEA.
claims.verbatim: The Alaska Department of Natural Resources (DNR) has issued a Preliminary Decision proposing to convey approximately 19,950 acres of State-owned land
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority (AIDEA)
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. The fact sheet is dated 'July 2026' with no day, so 2026-07-01 is a placeholder for the month. Case number is ADL 234762 and the comment deadline was August 19th. KTNA (October 19th) gives 'nearly 20,000 acres' with parcels in Houston, Meadow Lakes and Willow. The DNR notice it links (id=224431) wasn't fetched.

claims.claim: The Houston conveyance would be a no-land-value transfer under the state's public and charitable use statute.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority (AIDEA)
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. The table row on the page reads 'Statutory authority AS 38.05.810(a)' followed by an em dash and 'Public and Charitable Use'. The verbatim stops before the dash. The body says 'noncompetitive, no-land-value conveyance under Alaska Statute 38.05.810'. The site is about two miles north of Houston. This matches the October 26th hearing topic 'Public & Charitable Use Land Conveyances' (agenda not fetched, see killed).

claims.claim: AIDEA's own fact sheet says no specific end use for the Houston land has been selected.
claims.verbatim: This proposal is not a predetermined development project, and no specific end use has been definitively selected.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority (AIDEA)
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. The listed possibilities include 'utility, energy, and technology infrastructure' but not the words 'data center'. KTNA (October 19th) reports 'Possible uses include data centers, utility development and gravel extraction.'

claims.claim: DNR is still reviewing public comments on the Houston land transfer and the timeline for a decision is unclear.
claims.verbatim: the agency is reviewing public comments and working on a decision, although that timeline is unclear.
claims.source_outlet: KTNA (Marion Chesterton), published by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: Inside the window. Status as reported by DNR to KTNA. No primary DNR status document was fetched. Consistent with the AIDEA fact sheet: 'DNR reviews timely comments and issues a Final Finding and Decision'.

claims.claim: The Houston City Council and Meadow Lakes Community Council voted unanimously in July to oppose the transfer.
claims.verbatim: The Houston City Council and Meadow Lakes Community Council voted unanimously to oppose the transfer back in July.
claims.source_outlet: KTNA (Marion Chesterton), published by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: The votes are background (July) but were reported inside the window. Council minutes weren't fetched, so this is a single secondary source.

claims.claim: The Willow Area Community Council passed a resolution in September to send the Mat-Su Borough a letter opposing the transfer.
claims.verbatim: passed a resolution in September to send a letter to the Matanuska-Susitna Borough opposing the transfer
claims.source_outlet: KTNA (Marion Chesterton), published by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: Single secondary source. The council's letter wasn't fetched.

claims.claim: AIDEA director Randy Ruaro testified that no developer, tenant, power source or site plan exists for the Houston land.
claims.verbatim: testified that no developer, tenant, power source, or site plan exists for the land,
claims.suggested_phrasing: Ruaro told senators there's no developer, tenant, power source or site plan, KTUU reported
claims.notes: This is KTUU's paraphrase, not a direct quote. The page reads 'Updated Oct. 14, 2026, 4:36 PM AKDT', while the URL path says 10/15 (likely UTC), so it falls one day before the window and counts as update background for No.88. The testimony was at the October 8th joint committee meeting per the same article.

claims.claim: Ruaro called the rumored Houston data center implausible because there is no excess energy supply.
claims.verbatim: the rumored data center is "implausible" because there is no excess energy supply.
claims.notes: Only the word 'implausible' is a direct quote of Ruaro. Quote that single word only, and paraphrase the rest.

claims.claim: Senate Resources chair Cathy Giessel estimated the Houston land is worth about $14 million a year in state general fund revenue that would be forgone.
claims.verbatim: the land is worth roughly $14 million a year, which she claims would be foregone state general fund revenue.
claims.suggested_phrasing: Giessel estimates about $14 million a year in forgone revenue
claims.notes: This is a legislator's estimate, and KTUU itself writes 'she claims'. Attribute it. The KTUU article doesn't name her role; check her title (Senate Resources co-chair or chair) before printing it. Claim text names her role on the scout's reading only.

claims.claim: Giessel said the University of Alaska charges a private Mat-Su developer $586,740 a year to lease 829 acres.
claims.verbatim: She said the University of Alaska charges a private Mat-Su developer $586,740 a year to lease 829 acres.
claims.suggested_phrasing: Giessel compared it with the $586,740 a year the University of Alaska collects on 829 acres
claims.notes: Attributed comparison, no UA primary fetched. The scout's 'Terra' tenant name is not on the page, so don't name the developer. Sanity check: $586,740 / 829 is about $708 an acre a year. At that rate 19,950 acres would be about $14.1 million, which is consistent with Giessel's figure, but that arithmetic is ours and must not be printed as a source figure.

claims.claim: The joint committee's subpoena of DNR Commissioner John Crowther passed with five yes votes.
claims.verbatim: The subpoena passed with five yays.
claims.notes: Already covered by No.88 (October 16th), so it's context for the update. Sen. Rauscher emailed his 'yes' vote after losing his connection. Crowther skipped the October 8th meeting, saying 'the Governor's office has not given us permission to attend.'

claims.claim: The next committee meeting on the land transfer was scheduled for October 26th at 10 a.m.
claims.verbatim: The next meeting is scheduled for Oct. 26 at 10 a.m.
claims.notes: The BASIS agenda page (primary) returned HTTP 403 on both www.akleg.gov and akleg.gov, so the presenters (Crowther, AHFC's Brian Butcher), the ANCH LIO Denali Room and the time and location change are NOT verified by the fact-checker. The showrunner must record its own read of the page. Date and time agree with the showrunner's read.

claims.claim: NOAA's Alaska Fisheries Science Center is using FT-NIR spectroscopy coupled with trained machine learning models to read otolith rings and age fish.
claims.verbatim: coupled with trained machine learning models to efficiently read otolith rings
claims.source_outlet: NOAA Fisheries, Alaska Fisheries Science Center
claims.notes: BACKGROUND, October 7th, before the window. Q&A with Dr. Jamal Moss, Acting Director, AFSC. FT-NIR stands for 'Fourier Transform Near-Infrared (FT-NIR) Spectroscopy'. Also verified: 'Increased sample throughput allows us to process more fish ages'.

claims.claim: Ageing fish the traditional way means a scientist prepares the ear bones by hand and reads the rings under a microscope.
claims.verbatim: The traditional method requires that a scientist manually prepare the otoliths and read them with a microscope.
claims.source_outlet: NOAA Fisheries, Alaska Fisheries Science Center
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. Same page: 'We typically estimate fish age by counting rings on their otoliths, or earbones.'

claims.claim: Alaska produces more than half the seafood caught off the U.S. coast, with an average wholesale value of nearly $4.75 billion a year from 2020 through 2024.
claims.verbatim: with an average wholesale value of nearly $4.75 billion a year from 2020 through 2024
claims.source_outlet: NOAA Fisheries, Alaska Fisheries Science Center
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. Preceding words: 'Alaska produces more than half the seafood caught in waters off the coast of the United States'. This is a wholesale value, not an ex-vessel value.

claims.claim: In 2018 NOAA said FT-NIR reads an otolith in 30 to 50 seconds, more than 10 times faster than traditional methods, with preliminary pollock efficiency gains of 600 to 800 percent.
claims.verbatim: However, for pollock preliminary estimates of efficiency could improve by 600 percent to 800 percent.
claims.suggested_phrasing: NOAA's early estimate, in 2018, was that pollock ageing could get 600 to 800 percent more efficient
claims.notes: OLD BACKGROUND (July 30th, 2018), labelled as such. It's a preliminary projection. The page says 'machine-based technology' and does not say machine learning. The speed sentence ends 'more than 10 times faster than traditional methods'; its '30-50 seconds' uses an en dash on the page. AFSC scientist named is Dr. Thomas Helser, Age and Growth Program.

claims.claim: The USGS assessment spans three stratigraphic sequences, the Ellesmerian, the Beaufortian and the Brookian.
claims.verbatim: The stratigraphic scope of the assessment encompasses the entirety of three stratigraphic sequences—the Ellesmerian, Beaufortian, and Brookian sequences
claims.notes: Page 1. Ages per the same page: Devonian to Triassic Ellesmerian, Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous Beaufortian, Lower Cretaceous to Cenozoic Brookian. Read by the showrunner via scripts/fetch_pdf_text.py.

claims.claim: The USGS defined 8 assessment units in the Ellesmerian sequence, 7 in the Beaufortian and 6 in the Brookian.
claims.verbatim: For the Ellesmerian sequence, eight AUs were defined ... For the Beaufortian sequence, seven AUs were defined ... For the Brookian sequence, two Lower Brookian and four Upper Brookian AUs were defined
claims.notes: Page 2. Sums to the 21 of C06.

claims.claim: By the showrunner's sum of the Table 1 gas means, the Ellesmerian sequence holds 19,093 billion cubic feet of the undiscovered gas, the Beaufortian 32,013 and the Brookian 44,988.
claims.verbatim: Total undiscovered conventional oil and gas resources ... 17,326 66,357 276,681 96,094
claims.notes: Showrunner sum of each assessment unit's mean gas (associated plus nonassociated rows) in Table 1, pages 4 and 5. The three sums add to 96,094 BCFG, the Table 1 total, which checks the arithmetic. Means add across units; the F95 and F5 values do not, so no range is given per sequence.

claims.claim: By the showrunner's sum of Table 1, about 14,502 billion cubic feet of the undiscovered gas is associated with oil and about 81,592 billion cubic feet is not.
claims.verbatim: This estimate includes gas that is associated with oil accumulations (associated gas) as well as gas that is not associated with any large accumulation of oil (nonassociated gas).
claims.notes: Showrunner sum of the gas means in the Oil-type rows (associated) and Gas-type rows (nonassociated) of Table 1. Adds to 96,094.

claims.claim: The single largest gas mean among the 21 units is the Beaufortian Deformed Central unit, 12,921 billion cubic feet of gas found without oil.
claims.verbatim: Beaufortian Deformed Central AU 1.0 Oil 11 23 209 59 11 26 230 65 0 0 4 1Gas 2,487 9,310 36,871 12,921
claims.notes: Table 1, page 5, the Gas row mean.

claims.claim: The USGS puts the estimated ultimate recovery of Point Thomson field at 8 trillion cubic feet of gas.
claims.verbatim: Point Thomson field, which has an estimated EUR value of 8 TCFG
claims.notes: Page 1. A known accumulation, not part of the 96 tcf undiscovered.

claims.claim: Existing gas discoveries across the Brooks Range foothills range from 4 to 600 billion cubic feet, per the USGS.
claims.verbatim: gas accumulations distributed across the Brooks Range foothills, for which existing discoveries have EUR values that range from 4 to 600 billion cubic feet of gas (BCFG)
claims.notes: Page 1.

claims.claim: The USGS says several ways of bringing North Slope gas to market have been proposed, citing the Alaska LNG developer 8 Star Alaska.
claims.verbatim: Given the considerable size of the gas resources, several mechanisms for bringing the gas to markets have been proposed (Thomas and others, 1996; 8 Star Alaska, LLC, 2026).
claims.notes: Page 1; the reference list gives 8 Star Alaska, LLC, Alaska LNG website, alaska-lng.com.

claims.claim: The USGS gives the mean undiscovered oil of the province as 17,099 million barrels with a range of 3,044 to 46,617 million barrels.
claims.verbatim: The mean undiscovered oil resource is 17,099 million barrels of oil (MMBO), or 17 billion barrels of oil, with an F95–F5 range from 3,044 to 46,617 MMBO.
claims.notes: Page 4.

claims.claim: The USGS median, the F50, for undiscovered North Slope gas is 66,357 billion cubic feet, about 66.4 trillion.
claims.notes: Table 1 totals row, gas columns F95 F50 F5 Mean. The mean (96,094) sits above the median because the distribution has a long high tail.

claims.claim: North Slope exploration has historically focused on oil, which is carried across Alaska by pipeline toward markets, the USGS writes.
claims.verbatim: Petroleum exploration in the Northern Alaska Province historically has focused on oil resources, which are initially transported across Alaska by pipeline, for eventual delivery to markets
claims.notes: Page 1, the sentence before C09. The pipeline is the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System (route in assets/geo/ak-taps.geo.json, Alaska Energy Authority layer 13); the fact sheet does not name it.

claims.claim: The USGS dates the discovery of the Prudhoe Bay field to 1968.
claims.verbatim: the discoveries of the Prudhoe Bay field in 1968 (Morgridge and Smith, 1972)
claims.notes: Page 1.

killed.claim: STAK Energy plans 1 to 3 GW of on-site generation.
killed.why: Not on either DNR notice (223817, 224224), which give no capacity, and not in Anchorage Press, which says 'a gigawatt or more'. The development plan attachment returned 503. Use C24 instead.

killed.claim: DNR's notice describes a gas-fired AI and cloud campus worth more than $10 billion.
killed.why: The notices say 'modular high-performance computing units' and give no dollar figure. More than $10 billion survives only as the developer's claim (C25) and AI/cloud only as Anchorage Press framing (C26).

killed.claim: Alaska Public reported the 17.3 to 276.6 tcf range.
killed.why: The Alaska Public (KNBA) article doesn't contain the range. It's in the Beacon/ADN piece and the USGS fact sheet.

killed.claim: The F5 high case is 276.6 trillion cubic feet.
killed.why: USGS Table 1 gives 276,681 BCFG, which rounds to 276.7 tcf. 276.6 is a truncation by the Beacon. Corrected in C02.

killed.claim: The USGS or Interior itself calls this the first province-wide gas assessment.
killed.why: Neither the fact sheet nor Interior's release says 'first'. It survives only as the Alaska Beacon's characterization (C17), with attribution.

killed.claim: The agency compares the estimate to nearly three years of U.S. consumption in its documents.
killed.why: Not in the fact sheet or the release. It's an oral briefing remark by Alicia Lindauer as reported by two outlets (C16), and must be attributed to her.

killed.claim: Trump posted that Alaska LNG is a federal government project on October 19th.
killed.why: ADN (published October 20th) says Trump posted 'last week'. The exact date is unverified and the Truth Social primary wasn't fetched. C31 is undated.

killed.claim: ADN October 19th/20th reports the 20 million tonnes a year capacity and the $44.5B to $54.5B estimate.
killed.why: Not in that ADN article (it says Glenfarne cites up to $55 billion). Both figures survive from the Alaska Beacon via Alaska Public, October 15th (C32, C33).

killed.claim: Any annual gas burn for a 1 GW or 3 GW North Slope plant.
killed.why: No fetched source (DNR notices, Anchorage Press, Cole, Alaska Current, USGS, Interior) states one, and per instructions none was computed.

killed.claim: The STAK project could consume twice as much natural gas as urban Alaska's grid.
killed.why: This appears only in an Anchorage Press related-story teaser, not the article body. It refers to a '$500 million project' that conflicts with Boyle's more than $10 billion, and may be a different project. Excluded.

killed.claim: North Slope proven gas reserves are nearly 30 tcf (Alaska Current) or more than 35 tcf (Cole).
killed.why: The figures conflict. Use Interior's 'roughly 35 trillion cubic feet' of proven reserves (C12).

killed.claim: The University of Alaska's 829-acre tenant is named Terra.
killed.why: The tenant isn't named on the KTUU page. The page says only 'a private Mat-Su developer'.
